lessons.title: Creating Compost from On-Farm Waste
lessons.body:
Compost is the cheapest way to feed your soil. On one hectare, you can make enough compost to cover your beds by collecting waste you already have. Start by gathering 'browns' and 'greens'. Browns are dry, dead plant material like maize stalks, straw, dry leaves, and sawdust. Greens are fresh, moist materials like vegetable scraps, weeds (before they seed), grass clippings, and animal manure. Aim for a mix of 2 parts browns to 1 part greens by volume. For example, for every wheelbarrow of fresh greens, add two wheelbarrows of dry browns. Chop everything into pieces smaller than your hand to speed up decomposition.

Build your pile in layers about 15 cm thick, alternating browns and greens. Keep the pile as moist as a wrung-out sponge. If it's too dry, add water; if too wet, add more browns. Turn the pile every week to add air. The pile should heat up to 55-65Â°C within a few days. If it doesn't heat, it needs more greens or water. After 4-6 weeks of turning, the compost will cool down and turn dark, crumbly, and smell earthy. That's when it's ready.

You can make compost in a simple heap, a bin made from wire mesh, or even a pit. On a 1-hectare farm, set aside a 2m x 2m area for composting. Turn it with a fork or shovel. In dry areas, cover the pile with a tarp or banana leaves to keep moisture in. In rainy areas, cover it to prevent it from getting too wet. Add a handful of wood ash or lime if you have it to balance acidity.

Apply compost at 2-4 tonnes per hectare (about 2-4 kg per square meter) before planting. Spread it on the soil surface and mix it into the top 15 cm with a hoe or fork. Compost feeds your plants slowly and improves soil structure, helping sandy soils hold water and clay soils drain better. It also feeds earthworms and beneficial microbes. Making your own compost saves money and turns waste into a resource.

lessons.title: Applying Organic Fertilizers and Amendments
lessons.body:
Organic fertilizers come from plant or animal sources. They release nutrients slowly and improve soil health. Common ones include animal manure (cattle, goat, poultry, rabbit), bone meal, blood meal, fish emulsion, wood ash, and rock phosphate. Each has different nutrient levels. For example, poultry manure is high in nitrogen (about 3-5% N), while cattle manure is lower (about 1-2% N). Wood ash is rich in potassium and calcium but should be used sparingly (no more than 1 kg per 10 square meters per year) because it raises soil pH.

Before applying any manure, compost it first. Fresh manure can burn plants and carry weed seeds and pathogens. Composted manure is safer and more effective. Apply composted manure at 2-5 tonnes per hectare (2-5 kg per square meter) depending on soil needs. Spread it evenly and incorporate it into the top 15 cm of soil two weeks before planting. For a quick boost, you can make manure tea: put a sack of composted manure in a drum of water, let it steep for 3-5 days, then dilute the liquid 1:10 with water and pour it around plant bases.

Bone meal is a good source of phosphorus (about 15-20% P) and calcium. Apply it at 100-200 g per square meter when preparing beds, especially for root crops like carrots and onions. Blood meal is high in nitrogen (12-15% N) and can be used as a sidedressing at 50-100 g per square meter. Fish emulsion is a liquid fertilizer that can be diluted and sprayed on leaves or soil. Wood ash can be sprinkled lightly around plants that need potassium, like tomatoes and potatoes, but avoid using it on acid-loving plants.

Always test your soil before applying amendments. Too much of any nutrient can harm plants and waste money. For example, excess nitrogen causes leafy growth but few fruits. Excess phosphorus can lock up other nutrients. Mix different organic fertilizers to provide a balanced diet. A simple mix: 1 part poultry manure, 1 part bone meal, 1 part wood ash, and 3 parts compost. Apply this at 200-300 g per square meter. Store fertilizers in a dry place, away from moisture and sunlight.

lessons.title: Using Cover Crops for Nutrient Cycling
lessons.body:
Cover crops are plants grown not for harvest but to feed the soil. They protect the soil from erosion, suppress weeds, and add nutrients. On a 1-hectare vegetable farm, you can grow cover crops in between main crops or on resting beds. The best cover crops for African farms include legumes like cowpea, lablab, pigeon pea, groundnut, and mucuna (velvet bean). These fix nitrogen from the air into the soil through nodules on their roots. Non-legumes like sorghum, millet, and sunflower are good for biomass and deep rooting.

Plant cover crops after harvesting your main crop. For example, after maize, sow cowpea or lablab. Broadcast seeds at 20-30 kg per hectare for small-seeded legumes, or 50-70 kg per hectare for larger seeds like cowpea. Rake the soil lightly to cover the seeds. If rain is scarce, irrigate lightly until they establish. Legumes can fix 50-200 kg of nitrogen per hectare in 2-3 months. That's like getting free fertilizer.

When the cover crop is flowering but before it sets seed, cut it down. This is when nitrogen content is highest. Chop the plants into pieces and leave them on the soil surface as mulch, or dig them into the top 15 cm. The mulch will break down and release nutrients. If you dig it in, wait 2-3 weeks before planting your next crop to avoid nitrogen tie-up. You can also let some cover crops like mucuna produce seeds, then harvest and save them for next season.

Cover crops also improve soil structure. Their roots break up compacted soil and create channels for water and air. Deep-rooted crops like pigeon pea can reach 1-2 meters down, bringing up nutrients from subsoil. After a cover crop, your soil will be softer, darker, and full of earthworms. You can also use cover crops as fodder for livestock, but if you do, you remove nutrients from the field. So, either graze lightly or cut and carry, returning manure to the field. In dry areas, use drought-tolerant cover crops like cowpea and lablab. In wet areas, use mucuna and lablab. Always rotate cover crops with vegetables to break pest and disease cycles.

lessons.title: Testing and Adjusting Nutrient Levels
lessons.body:
You cannot manage what you do not measure. Soil testing tells you what nutrients your soil has and what it needs. In many African countries, you can send soil samples to a government agricultural lab or a private lab. A basic test costs about $10-30. If you cannot afford a lab test, you can use a simple soil test kit from an agro-dealer. These kits test for pH, nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). They come with instructions and color charts.

To take a soil sample, collect soil from 10-15 spots across your 1-hectare field. Use a clean spade or auger. Dig 15 cm deep for annual crops. Mix all the samples in a clean bucket. Take about 500 g of the mixed soil and send it to the lab or test it yourself. Test at least once a year, preferably before the main planting season. The results will give you a nutrient rating: low, medium, or high for each nutrient, plus pH.

pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is. Most vegetables grow best at pH 6.0-7.0. If pH is below 5.5, your soil is too acidic. Add agricultural lime at 1-2 tonnes per hectare to raise pH. If pH is above 7.5, add elemental sulfur or composted organic matter to lower it. Lime takes 2-3 months to work, so apply it well before planting. Wood ash also raises pH but use it carefully.

For nitrogen: if low, add composted manure or plant legumes. For phosphorus: if low, add bone meal or rock phosphate. For potassium: if low, add wood ash or compost. Always adjust based on test results. Do not guess. Over-fertilizing wastes money and can pollute water. Under-fertilizing reduces yields. Keep records of your test results and what you applied. Compare year to year. You can also do a simple 'jar test' to check soil texture: put soil in a jar with water, shake, and let it settle. Sand settles first, then silt, then clay. This tells you how well your soil holds water and nutrients. Adjust organic matter accordingly.

lessons.title: Foliar Feeding for Quick Deficiency Fixes
lessons.body:
Foliar feeding means spraying liquid fertilizer directly onto plant leaves. Plants absorb nutrients through their leaves faster than through roots. This is useful when you see signs of deficiency and need a quick fix. For example, yellowing between veins on older leaves means magnesium deficiency. Purple leaves mean phosphorus deficiency. Yellow edges on new leaves mean potassium deficiency. Foliar feeding can correct these in days, while soil applications take weeks.

You can make your own foliar feeds from local materials. A simple nitrogen boost: mix 1 cup of urine (aged for a week) with 10 liters of water. Spray on leafy vegetables like kale and spinach. For a balanced feed, mix 2 cups of compost tea with 10 liters of water. For potassium, mix 1 cup of wood ash in 10 liters of water, let it sit overnight, strain, and spray. For calcium, crush 2-3 eggshells, soak in 1 liter of vinegar for a week (it will bubble), then dilute 1:10 with water. Always test on a few plants first to avoid burning.

Spray early in the morning or late in the evening when it's cool. Avoid spraying in full sun or before rain. Use a knapsack sprayer or a hand sprayer. Set the nozzle to a fine mist. Spray both sides of the leaves until they are wet but not dripping. Repeat every 7-10 days until the deficiency is corrected. Do not overdo itâtoo much foliar feed can burn leaves. If you use commercial foliar fertilizers, follow the label instructions exactly. Common ones include NPK 20-20-20, calcium nitrate, and magnesium sulfate.

Foliar feeding is not a substitute for good soil fertility. Use it as a supplement. If your soil is healthy, plants will rarely need foliar feeds. But when a deficiency appears, it's a quick rescue. Keep a notebook to record what you sprayed, when, and how plants responded. This helps you learn. Also, foliar feeding can be combined with pest control. For example, add a few drops of liquid soap to help the spray stick to leaves. But do not mix foliar feeds with herbicides or other chemicals unless the label says it's safe.

lessons.title: Integrating Vermicompost and Compost Tea
lessons.body:
Vermicompost is compost made by earthworms. It is richer in nutrients than regular compost and full of beneficial microbes. To make vermicompost, you need a worm bin. You can use a old bathtub, a wooden box, or a plastic crate. Drill holes in the bottom for drainage and air. Fill it with bedding: shredded newspaper, cardboard, or dry leaves. Moisten the bedding. Add red wiggler worms (Eisenia fetida). You can buy them from a supplier or find them in old manure piles. One kilogram of worms can process 1 kg of food waste per day.

Feed the worms vegetable scraps, fruit peels, coffee grounds, and crushed eggshells. Do not feed them meat, dairy, oily foods, or citrus. Bury the food in the bedding to prevent flies. Keep the bin moist but not soggy. In 2-3 months, the bedding will turn into dark, crumbly vermicompost. Harvest it by pushing the compost to one side and adding fresh bedding and food to the other side. The worms will migrate to the new food. Scoop out the finished vermicompost. Apply it at 1-2 tonnes per hectare (1-2 kg per square meter) as a top dressing or mix into seed beds.

Compost tea is a liquid extract of compost. It is made by steeping compost in water. There are two types: aerobic and anaerobic. Aerobic tea is made by bubbling air through a mixture of compost, water, and a food source like molasses for 24-48 hours. Anaerobic tea is made by simply soaking compost in water for 1-2 weeks. Aerobic tea is ready faster and smells sweet. Anaerobic tea can smell foul but still works. To make anaerobic tea: put 1 part compost in 5 parts water in a drum. Stir daily. After 1-2 weeks, strain. Dilute 1:10 with water before spraying.

Use compost tea as a foliar spray or soil drench. Spray on leaves every 2 weeks to prevent diseases and supply nutrients. As a soil drench, pour 1 liter per plant around the base. Compost tea introduces beneficial microbes that outcompete pathogens. It also provides a small amount of nutrients. Combine vermicompost and compost tea for a powerful fertility program. Apply vermicompost to the soil and spray compost tea on leaves. This covers both soil and plant needs. Keep your worm bin in a shaded area, away from extreme heat or cold. With proper care, your worm population will multiply, and you can share or sell extra worms to other farmers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Soil Fertility & Nutrition for One Hectare

On a single hectare, soil fertility is not an input cost â it is the engine of your margin. For most vegetable growers in Africa, fertiliser and soil amendments represent 20â35% of variable costs, yet nutrient-use efficiency on smallholder plots often sits below 40%. Closing that gap is the fastest route to profit per square metre. This reference consolidates the practical rules behind the module: build organic matter on-farm, apply amendments where roots can reach them, keep nutrients cycling with cover crops, test before you spend, and use foliar and liquid products to correct deficiencies fast rather than guessing.

Treat every soil decision as a business decision. A kilogram of nitrogen that never reaches the root is cash lost. A compost heap that heats properly converts "waste" into a product worth real money. A cover crop that fixes nitrogen replaces a bag you would otherwise buy. The numbers below are drawn from FAO and international soil-fertility guidance, adapted to African smallholder and commercial conditions.

1. Creating Compost from On-Farm Waste

Compost is the cheapest bulk organic matter you will ever buy â because you make it. A well-built heap of 1.5 m Ã 1.5 m Ã 1 m can process roughly 1 tonne of mixed residues and yield 300â500 kg of finished compost in 8â12 weeks. Target a carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio of about 25â30:1, moisture of 50â60% (squeeze test: a few drops), and internal temperature of 55â65 Â°C for the first two weeks to kill weed seeds and pathogens. Turn when temperature drops below 45 Â°C.

For a one-hectare vegetable block, you need roughly 5â10 tonnes of compost per year to maintain organic matter â so build a three-bay system and keep it producing continuously, not in one seasonal burst.

Table 1. Typical C:N ratios and on-farm availability of common African smallholder compost feedstocks

Maize stover / stalks60:1CarbonChop to <5 cm; slow to break down
Cattle manure (fresh)20:1NitrogenExcellent activator; may carry weed seeds
Poultry litter10:1NitrogenUse sparingly; high ammonia, strong activator
Vegetable crop residues15â20:1NitrogenRemove diseased material first
Banana / plantain pseudostem35:1Carbon + moistureChop and mix; very high water content
Wood ashâMineralAdds K and raises pH; max 5% of heap

Source: FAO, On-farm composting methods (Land and Water Discussion Paper, 2003) and FAO Soils Portal, fao.org/soils-portal.

2. Applying Organic Fertilizers and Amendments

Where you place organic matter matters more than how much you spread. Banding compost or manure along the planting row concentrates nutrients in the root zone and can cut total volume by 30â50% compared with broadcasting, while delivering the same crop response. Incorporate within 24 hours of application to reduce nitrogen volatilisation and runoff.

Manures vary enormously. Poultry litter is roughly three times richer in nitrogen than cattle manure, so applying "a wheelbarrow per bed" of poultry litter where cattle manure was intended can burn seedlings. Match rate to source.

Source: FAO, Plant Nutrition for Food Security: A Guide for Integrated Nutrient Management (FAO Fertilizer and Plant Nutrition Bulletin 16, 2006), fao.org.

3. Using Cover Crops for Nutrient Cycling

Cover crops are the only input that pays you twice: they fix or scavenge nutrients and they protect the soil surface. Legumes such as cowpea, lablab, groundnut, and pigeon pea can fix 40â120 kg N/ha in a season, depending on biomass and inoculation. Non-legumes such as cereal rye, sorghum, or millet scavenge residual nitrogen and prevent leaching.

For vegetable rotations, plant a legume cover in the off-season or between cash crops, then terminate at 50% flowering and incorporate or leave as mulch. On a one-hectare plot, a strong cowpea cover can substitute for 1â2 bags of urea equivalent â a direct cash saving.

4. Testing and Adjusting Nutrient Levels

Do not guess. A single laboratory soil test (pH, organic carbon, N, P, K, and micronutrients) costs a fraction of one season's fertiliser budget and prevents over- or under-application. In the absence of a lab, use a soil test kit or send samples through your national agricultural research service. Sample at 0â20 cm depth, 15â20 sub-samples per hectare in a zig-zag pattern, mixed into one composite.

Key African benchmarks: most vegetable crops perform best at pH 6.0â6.8. Below pH 5.5, phosphorus locks up and aluminium becomes toxic â apply agricultural lime at 1â3 t/ha based on test recommendation. Above pH 7.5, iron and zinc deficiencies appear â use chelated foliar sprays rather than soil application.

5. Foliar Feeding for Quick Deficiency Fixes

Foliar feeding is a correction tool, not a base fertiliser programme. It works within 24â72 hours and is ideal for micronutrient deficiencies (iron, zinc, boron, manganese) and for rescuing a crop during a critical growth stage. Use low concentrations â typically 0.5â2% solution â and spray in the early morning or late afternoon to avoid leaf burn. Add a few drops of mild soap as a surfactant if no commercial spreader is available.

Foliar nitrogen (e.g., 1â2% urea solution) can give a visible greening response in 3â5 days, but it will not fix a phosphorus or potassium shortage. Diagnose first, then spray.

6. Integrating Vermicompost and Compost Tea

Vermicompost is finished compost that has passed through earthworms. It is finer, richer in available nutrients, and loaded with beneficial microbes. Apply it as a band at planting (200â500 g per plant for tomatoes and peppers) or as a top-dressing. Compost tea â made by steeping mature compost in aerated water for 24â36 hours â is a microbial inoculant, not a fertiliser. Use it to boost soil biology and suppress some foliar diseases, but do not rely on it to meet crop nutrient demand.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Compost and Manure Handling

Fresh manure and unfinished compost can carry E. coli, Salmonella, and parasitic eggs (including Ascaris). Never apply fresh manure to leafy vegetables within 90 days of harvest, or to root crops within 120 days. Always wear gloves and boots when handling manure, wash hands with soap after work, and ensure compost reaches 55â65 Â°C for at least three consecutive days before use on food crops. Do not use compost tea made from manure on edible plant parts. Keep children and animals away from active heaps.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Build the heap right: 25â30:1 C:N, 50â60% moisture, turn at 55â65 Â°C, finish in 8â12 weeks.
  • Band, don't broadcast: place compost and manure in the planting row to cut volume 30â50% with the same yield.
  • Know your manure: poultry litter is ~3Ã richer than cattle manure â adjust rates or you will burn seedlings.
  • Plant a legume cover in the off-season; cowpea or lablab can fix 40â120 kg N/ha.
  • Test soil annually (0â20 cm composite); target pH 6.0â6.8 for vegetables.
  • Lime acid soils at 1â3 t/ha based on test results; use chelates for micronutrients on alkaline soils.
  • Foliar feed only to correct â 0.5â2% solution, early morning or late afternoon, never as base nutrition.
  • Use vermicompost and compost tea as biology boosters and supplements, not as your main nutrient source.
  • Observe the 90/120-day rule for manure on leafy and root crops, and never compost-tea edible plant parts from manure.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO Soils Portal â soil fertility, organic matter, and nutrient management resources
  • FAO â On-farm composting methods (Land and Water Discussion Paper 2)
  • FAO â Plant Nutrition for Food Security: A Guide for Integrated Nutrient Management (Bulletin 16)
  • CGIAR â integrated soil fertility management research for African farming systems
  • IITA â soil health, cover crops, and legume rotation guidance for sub-Saharan Africa

Business note: Every tonne of compost you make on-farm replaces purchased inputs; every kilogram of nitrogen fixed by a cover crop is margin retained. Track compost produced, manure applied, cover-crop biomass, and soil test results in the same record book as your yields and sales. Soil fertility is not a cost centre â it is the balance sheet of your hectare.

quiz.q: What is the ideal ratio of browns to greens in a compost pile?
options: A) 1 part browns to 2 parts greens
B) 2 parts browns to 1 part greens
C) Equal parts browns and greens
D) 3 parts browns to 1 part greens
quiz.explanation: A 2:1 ratio of browns to greens provides the right carbon-to-nitrogen balance for efficient composting.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost pile?
quiz.explanation: Turning weekly adds oxygen and speeds up decomposition.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a compost pile does not heat up?
options: B) It needs more greens or water
C) It is ready to use
D) It has too much air
quiz.explanation: A lack of heat usually means insufficient nitrogen (greens) or moisture.

quiz.q: How much compost should you apply per hectare?
quiz.explanation: 2-4 tonnes per hectare (2-4 kg per square meter) is a typical application rate for vegetables.

quiz.q: Which of these is a 'green' material for composting?
quiz.explanation: Fresh grass clippings are moist and nitrogen-rich, making them a green material.

quiz.q: Why should fresh manure be composted before use?
options: A) To increase its nutrient content
B) To kill weed seeds and pathogens
quiz.explanation: Composting heats the manure enough to kill many weed seeds and harmful pathogens.

quiz.q: Which organic fertilizer is highest in nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Poultry manure contains about 3-5% nitrogen, higher than most other manures.

quiz.q: What is bone meal a good source of?
quiz.explanation: Bone meal is rich in phosphorus (15-20% P) and calcium.

quiz.q: How should wood ash be used?
options: A) In large amounts to raise pH
B) Sparingly because it raises pH
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is high in potassium and calcium but raises soil pH, so it should be used sparingly.

quiz.q: What is a simple mix of organic fertilizers for vegetables?
options: A) 1 part poultry manure, 1 part bone meal, 1 part wood ash, 3 parts compost
D) 1 part fresh manure, 1 part water
quiz.explanation: This mix provides a balance of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and organic matter.

quiz.q: Which cover crop is a legume that fixes nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Cowpea is a legume that forms nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

quiz.q: When is the best time to cut a cover crop for maximum nitrogen?
options: A) At flowering but before seed set
C) When it is a seedling
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen content is highest at flowering, before the plant uses nutrients for seed production.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen can a legume cover crop fix per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Legumes can fix 50-200 kg of nitrogen per hectare under good conditions.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of deep-rooted cover crops like pigeon pea?
options: B) They bring up nutrients from subsoil
quiz.explanation: Deep roots access nutrients leached below the topsoil and bring them to the surface.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after digging in a cover crop before planting the next crop?
quiz.explanation: Waiting 2-3 weeks allows the cover crop to decompose and prevents nitrogen tie-up.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH range for most vegetables?
quiz.explanation: Most vegetables grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, pH 6.0-7.0.

quiz.q: What should you add if your soil pH is below 5.5?
quiz.explanation: Lime raises pH, making acidic soil more neutral.

quiz.q: How many spots should you collect soil from for a composite sample?
quiz.explanation: Collecting from 10-15 spots gives a representative sample of the field.

quiz.q: What does a jar test measure?
quiz.explanation: A jar test separates sand, silt, and clay to determine soil texture.

quiz.q: If a soil test shows low phosphorus, what should you add?
quiz.explanation: Bone meal is a good source of phosphorus.

quiz.q: What is a sign of magnesium deficiency in plants?
options: B) Yellowing between veins on older leaves
C) Yellow edges on new leaves
quiz.explanation: Magnesium deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis on older leaves.

quiz.q: When is the best time to spray foliar feed?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Cooler times reduce evaporation and leaf burn.

quiz.q: How can you make a simple nitrogen foliar feed?
options: A) Mix 1 cup urine with 10 liters water
B) Mix 1 cup wood ash with 10 liters water
C) Mix 1 cup vinegar with 10 liters water
quiz.explanation: Aged urine diluted 1:10 with water provides a quick nitrogen boost.

quiz.q: How often should you repeat foliar feeding until deficiency is corrected?
quiz.explanation: Spraying every 7-10 days gives plants time to absorb nutrients without burning.

quiz.q: What is vermicompost?
options: C) A type of cover crop
quiz.explanation: Vermicompost is the product of earthworm digestion of organic waste.

quiz.q: What should you NOT feed to worms in a vermicompost bin?
quiz.explanation: Meat and dairy attract pests and smell bad in worm bins.

quiz.q: How long does it take to make vermicompost?
quiz.explanation: Worms process bedding and food into compost in about 2-3 months.

quiz.q: What is the difference between aerobic and anaerobic compost tea?
options: A) Aerobic is bubbled with air, anaerobic is not
B) Aerobic is smelly, anaerobic is sweet
quiz.explanation: Aerobic tea is aerated during brewing, while anaerobic tea is made without air.

quiz.q: How should compost tea be diluted before spraying?
quiz.explanation: Diluting 1:10 prevents burning and spreads microbes over a larger area.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using compost tea as a foliar spray?
options: B) It introduces beneficial microbes that outcompete pathogens
C) It provides high levels of NPK
D) It replaces all other fertilizers
quiz.explanation: Compost tea adds beneficial microorganisms that can suppress diseases.
